They have also inferred cosmological parameters directly from galaxy catalogs by treating galaxies as nodes. Such GNNs can learn which spatial scales and relations constrain the parameters, and they may find features beyond the usual two-point statistics.

The choice of architecture matters for each type of astronomical data, because each type has its own characteristics that suit some architectures better than others. A fully connected network is inefficient for image classification compared with a CNN, which uses the spatial structure of images. Researchers also combine modules, for example convolutional layers for local features with attention layers for long-range dependencies.

Neural network architectures and their inductive biases are becoming more important for astronomers. The field of architectures is evolving rapidly, and new designs combine computational principles with domain-specific knowledge. Astronomers should follow these developments and carefully evaluate their relevance to specific astronomical problems.

15.7 Bayesian Neural Networks

Backpropagation and SGD train a neural network efficiently. They lead only to a point estimate of the parameters, the vector \(\mathbf{w}\) that minimizes the empirical loss (the loss on the training data) \[ \mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} L(\mathbf{w}). \]

This is analogous to maximum likelihood estimation in linear regression (Chapter 4). It gives the best fit but no information about the uncertainty of the parameters. In Bayesian analysis we characterize the posterior distribution of the parameters, given by \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w}). \]

With the posterior we can make predictions that account for the uncertainty of the parameters. We integrate over the parameter values and obtain \[ p(y|\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D}) = \int p(y|\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D})\mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}. \]

In astronomy, this uncertainty is often as important as the prediction itself. It helps us tell confident predictions, based on ample evidence, from speculative ones where the model is uncertain.

One main limitation of neural networks, compared with the simpler models of the earlier chapters, is that Bayesian inference is difficult. For Bayesian linear regression we derived the posterior analytically (Chapter 5), so the inference was tractable. For neural networks, the nonlinear structure and the high dimension of the parameter space make the posterior intractable to compute exactly. A modern neural network can have millions or even billions of parameters, so sampling directly from its posterior is too costly.

Researchers have developed several practical approximations to Bayesian inference in neural networks. One of them, dropout, is simple to apply and also interesting in theory. It was introduced as a regularization technique, and its connections to Bayesian methods make it useful for uncertainty quantification.

Monte Carlo Dropout

In machine learning, training fits the weights of a neural network, and inference uses the trained network to predict on new data. During training, dropout sets the output of each neuron to zero with probability \(p\). It works in two steps.

  1. For each forward pass in training, we create a random mask for each neuron \(i\) such that \[ m_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1-p). \] Here \(m_i = 1\) means that the neuron stays active and \(m_i = 0\) means that it is removed for this pass. The Bernoulli distribution takes the value 1 with probability \(1-p\) and the value 0 with probability \(p\).

  2. We then apply the mask to the outputs of the layer and rescale them to get \[ \tilde{\mathbf{h}}^{(l)} = \mathbf{m} \odot \mathbf{h}^{(l)} / (1-p). \] The symbol \(\odot\) denotes the element-wise product of the mask \(\mathbf{m}\) and the layer outputs \(\mathbf{h}^{(l)}\). The factor \(1/(1-p)\) keeps the expected output of the layer the same in training and in inference. It is similar to the bias correction of the Adam optimizer, where we divide by \(1-\beta_1^t\) to correct the initialization bias of the moving averages. In both cases the division restores the expected value.

Dropout makes the network build redundant paths, so that the loss of a few neurons does little harm. It is like training a team whose members sometimes take sick leave. The team must learn to work well when some members are absent, so that no single person becomes a bottleneck. In the same way, the network does not rely too heavily on any single neuron or path, and this redundancy helps prevent overfitting. Figure 15.17 shows a neural network and the same network with some neurons dropped by a mask. Panel (c) shows Monte Carlo dropout, which we describe below.

In standard inference, the trained network predicts on new data with dropout typically turned off, so we use the full network. Training with dropout lets the network tolerate missing neurons, and the full network generally gives the most accurate predictions.

However, we can also keep dropout active in inference and perform multiple forward passes with different random masks. This technique is called Monte Carlo dropout. It approximates the Bayesian predictive integral above and gives uncertainty estimates in addition to predictions.

Monte Carlo dropout lets us sample different network configurations during inference. The predictions vary from pass to pass, and this variation gives insight into how confident the network is. If the predictions agree whichever neurons are dropped, we can trust them more. Large variations between the predictions suggest higher uncertainty.

Dropout has an ensemble learning view and a Bayesian view. In the ensemble view, dropout creates an implicit collection of neural networks. Each mask gives a different “thinned” network, a subnetwork of the original architecture. This is similar to bootstrap aggregating (bagging), which trains independent models on different bootstrap resamples of the data (Section 3.7). The spread of their predictions estimates the variance of the prediction, and the average of the predictions reduces it and improves generalization. With Monte Carlo dropout we use the thinned networks in the same way when we predict on new data.

This ensemble view connects directly to the Bayesian view. With dropout kept active in inference, multiple forward passes with different random masks effectively sample from an approximate posterior distribution over network functions. Each dropout mask gives a different neural network configuration, analogous to a sample from the posterior distribution of the weights. Averaging the predictions of these forward passes gives \[ p(y|\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D}) \approx \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T p(y|\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m}_t). \] Here \(T\) is the number of forward passes with different masks \(\mathbf{m}_t\).

This is an approximation to the predictive distribution that we would ideally compute by Bayesian model averaging. Bayesian model averaging is the average of the predictions over the possible parameter values, weighted by the posterior. The variance of these predictions is a measure of the model uncertainty, and we estimate it by \[ \text{Var}_{\mathbf{m}}[f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})] \approx \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T (f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m}_t) - \bar{f}(\mathbf{x}))^2. \] The function \(f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m}_t)\) is the prediction of the network with the mask \(\mathbf{m}_t\), and \(\bar{f}(\mathbf{x})\) is the mean of these predictions over the masks.

The uncertainty from Monte Carlo dropout mainly represents model uncertainty, also called epistemic uncertainty. It stems from the limited knowledge of the model, because of limited training data or model capacity. It differs from aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from the noise in the data itself. Even the model uncertainty alone is an improvement over standard deterministic neural networks, which give only point predictions with no indication of confidence.

The spread of the passes, drawn as a band in panel (c) of Figure 15.17, depends on the dropout probability \(p\). A larger \(p\) tends to widen the band. The value of \(p\) is a choice for the training and does not by itself measure our actual uncertainty. The band shows only the model uncertainty, so we add the noise of the data to it and count how often test observations fall inside. This shows whether a given \(p\) gives a band that is too narrow or too wide.

Beyond Dropout

Dropout is only an approximation to Bayesian inference. It can fail to reproduce the complete predictive distribution, especially far from the training data or when the uncertainty is highly structured. Panel (c) of Figure 15.17 shows this far from the data, where the band stays narrow but the mean departs from the function. The dropout masks add diversity to the predictions, but they do not explore the parameter space well enough to represent the posterior distribution. This has spurred research into full Bayesian approaches to neural networks.

One direction of this research adapts the MCMC methods of Chapter 13 to sample from the posterior distribution of the network weights. However, the high dimension of the weight space makes these methods computationally costly.

An alternative is variational inference, which turns a sampling problem into an optimization problem. We assume a simple parametric form for the posterior distribution of the weights, such as a Gaussian, and optimize its parameters instead of sampling. We can then sample weights from this distribution to predict with uncertainty. Variational inference is a central idea in statistical inference, but its detailed application to neural networks is technical, so we only describe the idea.

Standard and Bayesian neural networks show a trade-off that we met in Chapter 14, between low computing cost and uncertainty quantification. Standard neural networks are efficient, because backpropagation and SGD handle massive data sets and complex functions. The main limitation of neural networks is their uncertainty quantification. It is not well understood, or at least not easy to achieve or to derive analytically. The blanket criticisms of their interpretability matter less.

The lack of uncertainty quantification has led modern research in two directions. One is to make classical Bayesian models like Gaussian processes more scalable. For instance, neural networks can take over some computational components, so that we pay their cost once in training. The core of such a model remains Bayesian linear regression in a feature space (Chapter 14). The other is to develop full Bayesian approaches for neural networks themselves. Both directions have progressed in recent years.

15.8 Beyond A Fancy Interpolator

A common misconception is that neural networks are merely fancy interpolation methods that only fit the training points, without theoretical grounding. This view overlooks the mathematical properties of neural networks and the theoretical advances that explain in part why and how they work. Giving the proofs is beyond the scope of this book, but we highlight three developments. They give insight into learning, generalization and computation in neural networks.

Double Descent

Double descent became widely known in deep learning around 2019. It runs against classical statistical learning theory and our intuitions about generalization and the complexity of a model. In classical statistical learning we expect a U-shaped test error curve, as in panel (a) of Figure 15.4 (Section 4.7). As the complexity increases, the performance first improves, because the model fits the real patterns in the data. It then deteriorates, because the model starts to overfit. This is the bias-variance tradeoff between underfitting and overfitting.

Neural networks can violate this classical expectation. After the initial overfitting phase, the performance can improve again as the complexity increases, which gives a double descent pattern in the test error curve. Models can then have far more parameters than training examples, and we call them overparameterized. Even so, they can avoid the severe overfitting that classical theory predicts. We illustrated this phenomenon earlier in panel (b) of Figure 15.4.

One explanation of this phenomenon concerns how the solution space changes as we add parameters. In classical optimization, adding parameters may create more local minima, so the global minimum becomes harder to find. In neural networks, however, the solution space may change at some point. Beyond that point the solutions may be more connected, with paths between what were isolated local minima. Gradient descent can then move between solutions more easily and gradually find better minima that may have been out of reach in lower dimensions. This may let the network find better solutions even with many more parameters than training examples.

Figure 15.18 gives a toy example. In panel (a) one parameter gives two isolated minima with a barrier between them. In panel (b) a second parameter turns them into a ring-shaped valley, like the brim of a Mexican hat. A path along the valley avoids the barrier.

Neural Tangent Kernel

Another theoretical advance, popular since about 2018, is the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). It connects neural networks to kernel methods such as the Gaussian processes of Chapter 14. Recall that a kernel is the inner product of feature vectors, \(k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}')\). For a neural network with one output the features are the gradients of the output with respect to the weights. The NTK is the inner product of these gradients at the initial weights for two inputs, \(\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} f_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x})^T \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} f_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}')\).

Consider the limit of infinite width, where the number of neurons in each hidden layer goes to infinity. In this limit the behavior of a neural network during training can be described by a kernel function. This kernel depends only on the network architecture and the initialization. It does not change with the parameter values during training.

The NTK gives one reason why gradient descent in overparameterized neural networks can find good solutions although the loss function is non-convex. In the infinite-width limit, each parameter changes only slightly during training. The network output is then linear in the parameters near the initial values, so the squared-error loss is convex. Gradient descent can then reach a global minimum of the training loss.

In the infinite-width limit, a neural network behaves like a kernel method with a fixed kernel. Its kernel is defined by the architecture, whereas for Gaussian processes we choose the kernel a priori. As for Gaussian processes, a kernel can implicitly map the inputs to an infinite-dimensional feature space and still keep the computation tractable. A neural network of finite width can change its features during training and so learn the feature representation from the data.

The NTK also helps explain why some architectures work better than others for specific problems. Different architectures induce different kernel functions, which have different inductive biases. This lets us reason about the design of a neural network in terms of the properties of the induced kernel, as well as empirically. From a statistical perspective, the NTK gives a way to analyze the convergence and generalization properties of neural networks.

Grokking

Grokking is a phenomenon that bears on a question about learning. The question is whether neural networks only memorize the training examples or extract the underlying patterns. The term “grokking” borrows the concept of deep intuitive understanding from the science fiction author Robert A. Heinlein. Grokking suggests the second possibility.

One definition of intelligence is the ability to generalize beyond what was taught. It means to extract underlying principles and apply them to new situations. This ability separates rote memorization from learning the principle behind the examples, and it is characteristic of human cognition. Grokking suggests that neural networks can show a similar ability.

Consider neural networks trained on algorithmic tasks, for example modular addition, \((a + b) \mod c\), the remainder of \(a + b\) after division by \(c\). At first, these neural networks appear to memorize the training examples. They reach 100 percent training accuracy but generalize poorly to unseen examples. With continued training and weight decay, the networks suddenly “grok” the underlying pattern and reach a test accuracy close to 100 percent.

The internal representations change at this transition. While a neural network memorizes, the embedding of the inputs, which gives each input value a learned vector, tends to look irregular. After it groks the pattern, the embedding becomes structured and matches the mathematical properties of the task. For modular arithmetic, this embedding becomes periodic in the residue and puts most of its Fourier power on a few frequencies. This indicates that the network has discovered the mathematical structure instead of memorizing individual cases. Figure 15.19 shows the accuracy and the internal representations before and after grokking.

Grokking occurs even when neural networks have far more parameters than training examples, a regime where classical theory would predict memorization. Yet these neural networks eventually discover generalizable patterns, which suggests that learning in neural networks goes beyond interpolation between training points. The implications of grokking reach past simple arithmetic tasks. We may see related behavior in large language models, which can generalize in unexpected ways. For instance, models trained mostly on English text can generate coherent responses in languages that they saw very little in training, given relatively few examples. This suggests that these models extract linguistic patterns that hold across languages, instead of memorizing the training data.

Neural networks can also perform counterfactual generalization, which means combining concepts that did not occur together in training. Humans can imagine new combinations of concepts, and modern neural networks can generate coherent representations of such combinations. This recombination of learned elements is more than memorization.

Phenomena like grokking suggest that neural networks can go beyond memorization and learn the underlying patterns and principles of the data. Used with an understanding of how they work, they are useful tools for astronomical research and may find patterns and relationships that standard methods miss.

15.9 Foundation Models

Grokking suggests that neural networks can generalize beyond their training examples. We can use this ability in two steps. First, we pre-train one large model on extensive and varied data, usually without labels because labels are scarce in astronomy. Second, we fine-tune it, which means that we continue its training briefly on the data of the specific application. This replaces training a specialized neural network from scratch for each task, and we pay the high computing cost of pre-training only once. Reusing a pre-trained model for a new task in this way is called transfer learning.

A pre-trained model is a foundation model only if its representation transfers well enough to new tasks for few-shot learning, which we describe below.

Few-Shot Learning

A foundation model can learn from very few examples. This ability is called few-shot learning, and zero-shot learning when no example is needed. On a new task it can need far fewer examples than a model trained from scratch. A model pre-trained on a vast corpus of text and images can adapt to classify astronomical objects after a handful of examples from each category. This suggests that pre-training gives the model general knowledge about the structure of data in many domains, beyond a memory of its training data. Figure 15.20 compares this route with training a separate model from scratch for each task.

Many pre-trained models do not reach few-shot performance, because pre-training alone does not give a representation that is useful for a new task. Testing transfer needs care. A model trained and tested on objects from the same survey can score well. This shows generalization to similar data and does not show transfer. For transfer we test on data that differ in a way that matters, such as a different instrument, a different population or a different task.

Where labels are plentiful, a model trained directly on the task can already do well. It is then the baseline that a foundation model has to beat. The case for foundation models is strongest where labels are scarce.

Few-shot learning helps in astronomy, where labeled examples of rare phenomena can be scarce. A model pre-trained on broader astronomical data might need only a few examples of a rare event to identify other instances. Rare events include a particular type of stellar explosion and an unusual galaxy merger. This could speed up the discovery and classification of rare phenomena in the massive data sets of modern observatories. Simulations can supply labels where real ones are rare. A model trained on them must still cross the gap to real observations, which is itself a transfer problem.

Scientific Discovery

Pre-trained models also open possibilities for scientific discovery. When we model a complex phenomenon with a neural network, we want more than a fit of the observed data points. We want the underlying physical laws or patterns.

Astronomers have long read their data through heuristics built by hand, such as colors, line indices and fitted templates. Each is a compression chosen in advance. A representation learned from the data could in principle recover the compact description that the physics implies and that we have not written down. Present models fall well short of this. It remains the right aim, because it separates automating the measurements we already make from finding the variables we should have been measuring.

For astronomers, neural networks could then give more than efficient data processing. We would examine what the networks learn, both their outputs and their internal representations. We might then gain new insight into physical laws that are hard to find by traditional analysis.

A Common Error

The label foundation model is easy to misuse. A common error is to train a Transformer or another large architecture on one task and to call the result a foundation model. The architecture and the size are only the means. What counts is a representation that transfers to new instruments, populations or tasks. Without it, the model is only pre-trained and large, and the name foundation model overstates what it does.

15.10 Autoencoders: Nonlinear Dimension Reduction

A foundation model learns a representation of its training data, usually without labels. Learning a representation without labels is unsupervised learning. So far we used neural networks for supervised learning, where we learn a mapping from inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) to targets \(y\). In unsupervised learning we have the inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) alone and no targets \(y\).

Chapters 10 and 11 taught classical methods for this case. Principal component analysis (PCA) reduces the dimension, K-means clusters the data and Gaussian mixture models estimate densities. These methods rest on linear algebra and statistical principles, and their assumptions limit them. Neural networks extend them, keeping their ideas and relaxing their restrictive assumptions.

PCA as the Linear Case

PCA is the linear method that the autoencoder generalizes. For centered data \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) it finds a linear map \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times D}\) to a representation \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M\) with \(M < D\). We obtain this map from the directions of maximum variance, which are the eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix \[ \mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T. \] The rows of \(\mathbf{W}\) are the eigenvectors with the \(M\) largest eigenvalues, so \(\mathbf{W}\) is the transpose of the matrix \(\mathbf{B}_M\) of Chapter 10. The projection \[ \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} \] keeps as much variance as possible in the lower-dimensional space.

The reconstruction of PCA uses the transpose of the projection matrix \[ \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{z}. \] This is the best linear approximation of the original data from the compressed representation. Its reconstruction error is \[ E = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_i\|^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_i\|^2. \] This error is the information that the compression loses. Minimizing it is equivalent to maximizing the variance that the projection preserves, as Chapter 10 shows.

For \(M = D\) the rows of \(\mathbf{W}\) are \(D\) orthonormal eigenvectors, so \(\mathbf{W}\) is orthogonal and \(\mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{W}\) is the identity. The error is then zero and nothing is compressed. The strategy of PCA is therefore to keep only some of the components, with \(M < D\), and still most of the information. The error measures the small loss of information that we accept for a large gain in compression.

PCA has a closed-form solution through the eigendecomposition, but it is limited to linear transformations. This limit matters when the data lie on a nonlinear manifold, a curved surface of lower dimension in the high-dimensional space. For example, the Swiss roll is a two-dimensional sheet curled up in three dimensions. Linear projections have difficulty unfolding it. An autoencoder can use nonlinear transformations to describe the roll with two numbers for each point.

The Autoencoder

Autoencoders replace the linear transformations of PCA with nonlinear neural networks. They keep the goal of PCA, a low-dimensional representation with minimal reconstruction error. The nonlinear transformations can represent complex geometric relationships in the data.

PCA encodes with \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}\) and decodes with \(\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W}^T\mathbf{z}\). An autoencoder has the same two parts, an encoder and a decoder.

The encoder \(e(\mathbf{x})\) maps the input to a low-dimensional representation \[ \mathbf{z} = e(\mathbf{x}). \]

The decoder \(d(\mathbf{z})\) gives the reconstruction of the input from this representation \[ \hat{\mathbf{x}} = d(\mathbf{z}). \]

Both functions \(e(\mathbf{x})\) and \(d(\mathbf{z})\) are neural networks, and their architecture can vary with the data type and the task. Figure 15.21 shows an autoencoder made of fully connected layers.

A simple encoder with two layers is \[ e(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma_2(\mathbf{W}_2\sigma_1(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2), \] where \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are nonlinear activation functions such as GELU. The matrices \(\mathbf{W}_1\) and \(\mathbf{W}_2\) and the vectors \(\mathbf{b}_1\) and \(\mathbf{b}_2\) are the learnable parameters. The decoder \(d(\mathbf{z})\) has a similar structure with its own weight matrices and bias vectors. The encoder and the decoder are learnable functions, and their nonlinear layers can represent complex relationships in the data.

This is only one possible implementation. In practice we often use Convolutional Neural Networks for image data and Transformers for sequential data. The architecture encodes the inductive biases that we want for the data. The autoencoder concept stays the same for any building blocks.

We train an autoencoder with an objective that parallels the reconstruction error of PCA \[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i - d(e(\mathbf{x}_i))\|^2. \] This is the average squared distance between the input and its reconstruction after passing through the encoder and the decoder. We optimize all the weights of both networks.

Backpropagation works on any differentiable computational graph, so it gives the gradients of this loss with respect to all parameters. We update them by gradient descent as in supervised learning. Only the loss differs, because we minimize a reconstruction error.

Suppose that the encoder and the decoder are single-layer linear networks without activation functions \[\begin{aligned} e(\mathbf{x}) &= \mathbf{W}_e\mathbf{x} \\ d(\mathbf{z}) &= \mathbf{W}_d\mathbf{z}, \end{aligned}\] and that we minimize the reconstruction error. The encoder then converges to the PCA projection matrix up to an invertible \(M \times M\) matrix. The product \(\mathbf{W}_d\mathbf{W}_e\) converges to the PCA reconstruction map \(\mathbf{W}^T\mathbf{W}\). In this sense a linear autoencoder is equivalent to PCA. The nonlinear autoencoder extends PCA to more complex data structures.

An autoencoder has the shape of an hourglass, as Figure 15.21 shows, because the bottleneck dimension \(M\) is smaller than \(D\). The encoder reduces the dimension layer by layer until the bottleneck layer, which holds the low-dimensional latent representation \(\mathbf{z}\) (Section 6.5). The decoder then expands the dimension symmetrically back to the original one. The bottleneck is the constraint that drives the learning. Without it the network could copy the inputs to the outputs and extract no useful features. With it the network must keep the aspects of the data that matter most for an accurate reconstruction.

This compression resembles the way in which PCA finds principal components. PCA keeps the directions of maximum variance, and the bottleneck keeps the structure that matters most for the reconstruction. Autoencoders add nonlinear transformations to this idea.

The compressed representations can reveal features that we can interpret, much as PCA vectors can show physically meaningful directions in data space. In face images the latent dimensions might encode pose, lighting, expression and identity. In galaxy images they could correspond to physical properties such as morphological type, size, orientation and brightness. The training does not ask for these features.

We can examine a latent space in two simple ways. We can plot two latent coordinates for many objects and color each point by a measured property, such as the stellar mass of a galaxy. We can also change one latent coordinate, decode the result and see which features of the image change. A coordinate that follows a known property may carry a physical meaning.

Applications in Astronomy

Autoencoders have practical applications in astronomy beyond dimension reduction. One of them is denoising. Consider astronomical images with noise from cosmic rays, readout noise or sky background fluctuations. Noise typically lacks the structured correlations of the signal, so the bottleneck cannot encode it efficiently. The autoencoder then tends to keep the structured signal in its reconstruction and to discard the random noise.

A denoising autoencoder takes noisy inputs and targets clean outputs. We need pairs of noisy and clean examples, which can come from simulations or controlled observations. With such pairs we minimize \[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{clean}} - d(e(\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{noisy}}))\|^2. \] This loss trains the network to remove the noise and to keep the underlying signal.

A denoising autoencoder does not create new information or “generate more photons” from the observations. In Bayesian terms, a neural network trained with the squared error estimates the posterior mean of the clean signal given the noisy data. The network weights encode a prior on the signal through the training on similar examples. Denoising is useful for visual analysis and pattern recognition. The cleaned output is our best guess from prior knowledge, and it adds no observational data.

In astronomy it is tempting to read denoised results as “super-resolution” or “enhanced signal-to-noise”. Denoising has worked well for cleaning astronomical images, spectra and time series. We must not treat the results as if they held more observational information than the original data.

Autoencoders can also find anomalies or outliers. We train the autoencoder on a data set of “normal” examples. Instances with a large reconstruction error are then likely outliers, because they do not follow the regularities that the autoencoder learned. The technique has been used to detect unusual astronomical objects, instrument failures and data quality problems.

In all these applications the advantage of autoencoders over PCA is that they can represent nonlinear relationships. Astronomical data often have nonlinear structure. Galaxy morphologies form complex manifolds in image space, and light curves of variable stars show nonlinear variation in time. Autoencoders can find this structure, and this can lead to more efficient compression, better denoising and more accurate anomaly detection.

15.11 Domain Transfer and Cross-Modal Learning

An autoencoder maps an input back to itself through a bottleneck. The same encoder-decoder structure can go beyond this self-reconstruction and relate different data domains to each other. The extension rests on the bottleneck layer, which holds a meaningful representation of the main structure of the input. This latent representation drops superficial details and keeps the patterns that define the data. If it encodes the “knowledge” or “semantics” of the data, it should help with tasks beyond simple reconstruction.

We generalize the autoencoder by keeping the encoder \(e(\mathbf{x}) \rightarrow \mathbf{z}\) and allowing different uses of the latent representation \(\mathbf{z}\). The decoder no longer needs to reconstruct the original input. We can train it to produce outputs in different domains or modalities, which are types of data such as images and spectra. The encoder \(e(\cdot)\) and the decoder \(d(\cdot)\) remain neural networks, but we may design their architectures for the specific input and output. This gives two uses in astronomy, domain transfer and cross-modal learning.

Domain Transfer

Domain transfer maps between different representations of similar data. It differs from transfer learning (Section 15.9), where we reuse a pre-trained model for a new task. An autoencoder follows the pattern \(\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{z} \mapsto \mathbf{x}\). Domain transfer follows the pattern \(\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{z} \mapsto \mathbf{y}\), where \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) belong to related but distinct domains. The two steps are \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{z} &= e(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{y} &= d(\mathbf{z}). \end{aligned}\]

One application in astronomy reduces the gap between simulated and observed data. In stellar spectroscopy, theoretical atmospheric models predict stellar spectra from physical parameters such as temperature, surface gravity and metallicity. However, these simulations often miss some physical processes. Missing opacity sources, incomplete line broadening mechanisms and simplified atmospheric assumptions create systematic differences between predicted and observed spectra.

An encoder-decoder network can learn these systematic differences from pairs of simulated and observed spectra. The encoder obtains the physical information from the simulated spectrum. The decoder translates this information into a more realistic observed spectrum. The latent space \(\mathbf{z}\) still encodes the physical parameters, but the output \(d(\mathbf{z})\) matches the observations better than the direct simulation does.

Our simulations are imperfect approximations of physical processes. Instead of discarding these models, domain transfer can correct the systematic differences and keep the physical basis of the models. The resulting hybrid model joins the theory built into the simulations with empirical corrections learned from data.

We can use this correction to measure the parameters of stars from their observed spectra. We choose calibration stars whose physical parameters, such as temperature, surface gravity and metallicity, we trust. For each of them we pair the simulated spectrum, computed from its parameters, with the observed spectrum, and the network learns the correction. For a new star we vary the parameters until the spectrum that we simulate and correct with the network matches the observed spectrum. The parameters that give the best match are our estimates. They should be better than those of a fit with the pure simulations, if the new star resembles the calibration stars.

Domain transfer also gives predictions across wavelengths. We can train a neural network to predict infrared galaxy spectra from optical observations, or to generate radio emission maps from optical images. These predictions are educated guesses based on learned correlations and carry no new physical information. They can still guide observing plans and help identify promising targets for follow-up studies.

Cross-Modal Learning

Cross-modal learning requires several data modalities to share one latent representation. Instead of a mapping between two spaces, different data types encode into and decode from the same latent space. For two modalities, the encoders and decoders are \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{z}_1 &= e_1(\mathbf{x}_1) \\ \mathbf{z}_2 &= e_2(\mathbf{x}_2) \\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 &= d_1(\mathbf{z}) \\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_2 &= d_2(\mathbf{z}). \end{aligned}\]

Each modality has its own encoder and decoder, but all modalities share the same latent representation \(\mathbf{z}\). The training objective typically asks for the reconstruction of each modality from itself. For one object seen in both modalities we require \(\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{z}_2 = \mathbf{z}\), or we add a penalty on \(\|\mathbf{z}_1 - \mathbf{z}_2\|^2\) to the loss, so that \(\mathbf{z}_1 \approx \mathbf{z}_2 \approx \mathbf{z}\). The network must then find one representation of the information that the modalities share.

Consider galaxy images and galaxy spectra that we encode into the same latent space. The image encoder \(e_1\) must extract information from morphological features, colors and spatial structure. The spectrum encoder \(e_2\) must extract information from spectral lines, continuum shapes and emission features. Both encoders map to the same latent space. Figure 15.22 compares this shared latent space with domain transfer.

The shared representation can reflect the physical properties that affect both modalities. For instance, the stellar population age influences both the color of a galaxy in images and the strength of specific absorption features in its spectrum. The stellar mass affects both the apparent size of the galaxy and its overall spectral energy distribution. Because the latent space must represent both modalities, the network can find these physical relationships without explicit supervision.

Cross-modal learning can do three things. Each modality can be reconstructed from itself, as in an autoencoder. The network can predict one modality from the other, for example by generating spectra from images or the reverse. It can also discover latent variables that correspond to shared physical properties.

The tests that we described for autoencoders are more informative in a shared latent space. We can change one latent coordinate and decode it into every modality. This shows how different observational signatures of the same phenomenon are related.

Combining observations from many instruments, surveys and wavelength regimes is a long-standing problem in astronomy. Cross-modal learning addresses it, because objects are routinely observed with multiple instruments. Large surveys already provide both imaging and spectroscopic data for millions to billions of galaxies, and future facilities will generate multi-wavelength observations at larger scales. By learning shared representations from these observations, we analyze the data types together instead of in isolation. We can then discover the physical properties that show up in the different modalities.

15.12 Mixture Density Networks

Neural networks can also model a density. Instead of fitting a deterministic curve, a neural network can model the full probabilistic structure of the data. Standard supervised neural networks have a limitation. They assume a deterministic mapping that gives one output \(\mathbf{y}\) for each input \(\mathbf{x}\). This assumption frequently breaks down in scientific applications, where one-to-many mappings arise.

One-to-Many Relationships

We take a cross-section of the Swiss roll, but now as a supervised learning task. The data points form a folded structure in which a single input value \(x\) corresponds to several distinct output values \(y\). A standard neural network that predicts \(y\) from \(x\) with the mean squared error fails to represent this structure.

The network learns the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[y|x]\) at each input, which averages over all possible outputs for that input. This averaging smooths out the multimodal structure of the true distribution. The prediction may then correspond to no realistic outcome. At an input where three distinct output values are possible, the network predicts their average weighted by probability, which might be an impossible configuration. Panel (a) of Figure 15.23 shows this prediction for the Swiss roll.

One-to-many relationships are common in astronomy and other sciences. A cosmological simulation with fixed physical parameters gives a different realization for each random seed, with the same statistics but different individual structures. Several galaxy types can share the same stellar mass and differ in morphology, metallicity or star formation history. These examples show that a single output for each input is rare in complex scientific domains. A deterministic mapping is not enough here. Instead of a function \(y = f(x)\) with a single prediction, we need a model of the distribution of all possible outcomes given the input.

This need leads to density estimation, which has two forms. Unconditional density estimation learns the probability density \(p(\mathbf{x})\) of the data, as the Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) of Chapter 11 do. Conditional density estimation learns \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\) instead, and supervised problems with one-to-many relationships need it. The conditional density describes how the distribution of \(\mathbf{y}\) varies with \(\mathbf{x}\). It represents the range of possible outputs for each input through a probability distribution. It is of the same kind as the likelihood of Bayesian inference, a conditional distribution of the data.

Modeling \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\) instead of the joint distribution \(p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\) also has a computational advantage. The joint distribution of a complex structure such as the Swiss roll would be hard to describe. However, if we fix \(\mathbf{x}\) and look at the distribution of \(\mathbf{y}\), we often find a simpler and more tractable structure.

GMMs describe complex multimodal distributions by representing multiple peaks. This is the structure that we see in one-to-many mappings. However, a standard GMM has one main limitation. It models a single static distribution \(p(\mathbf{y})\) instead of a distribution \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\) that varies with the input. Consider one GMM for \(p(\mathbf{y})\) at all values of \(\mathbf{x}\) in the Swiss roll.

This model must represent all \(y\) values that occur anywhere in the range of \(x\). It averages out the distinct local patterns at specific \(x\) values. We need a GMM whose parameters change as functions of \(\mathbf{x}\). These parameters are the means, the covariances and the mixture weights.

These parameters should change gradually and smoothly. When two inputs \(\mathbf{x}_1\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2\) are similar, the conditional distributions \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}_1)\) and \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}_2)\) should also be similar. This assumption of local smoothness is physically reasonable, and it makes the computation easier.

Model and Training

This idea leads to Mixture Density Networks (MDNs), which combine neural networks with mixture models for conditional density estimation. A neural network computes the parameters of a GMM as functions of the input \(\mathbf{x}\). The resulting model can represent complex multimodal distributions that vary smoothly across the input space. Panels (b) and (c) of Figure 15.23 show the conditional density of such a neural network.

An MDN models \(p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\) as a mixture of Gaussians \[ p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k(\mathbf{x}) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k(\mathbf{x})), \] where \(\pi_k(\mathbf{x})\) are the mixture weights, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{x})\) the means and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k(\mathbf{x})\) the covariance matrices. All of them vary with the input \(\mathbf{x}\).

By the universal approximation property, a neural network can represent these functions, and we learn them directly from data. No prior knowledge of the true functional forms is needed.

For a mixture with \(K\) components in a \(D\)-dimensional output space, the network outputs \(K\) mixture weights \(\pi_k(\mathbf{x})\), which must sum to 1. It outputs \(K \times D\) mean values \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{x})\), one \(D\)-dimensional mean vector for each component. It also outputs the covariance parameters of each component, and we often simplify the covariances to diagonal matrices. Figure 15.24 shows the network and the mixture that it produces.

We train an MDN by maximum likelihood, as in Chapters 4 and 7. Given \(N\) input-output pairs \(\{(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^N\), we maximize the log-likelihood \[ \ell(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln p(\mathbf{y}_i|\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln \left[ \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k(\mathbf{x}_i) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{x}_i), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k(\mathbf{x}_i)) \right], \] where \(\mathbf{w}\) are the parameters of the neural network. We optimize them with the gradient-based methods of the earlier sections of this chapter.

The mixture weights \(\pi_k(\mathbf{x})\) must be non-negative and sum to one. We apply a softmax function (Chapter 8) to the corresponding network outputs, so that \[ \pi_k(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(z_k(\mathbf{x}))}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(z_j(\mathbf{x}))}, \] where \(z_k(\mathbf{x})\) are the raw network outputs. The means can take any value, so they need no transformation. The variances must be positive, so we typically apply an exponential function or the softplus function \(\ln(1 + e^{z})\) to the relevant network outputs. Numerical stability requires log-probabilities, because the product of many small probabilities can cause underflow (Chapter 7). The objective function is then the negative log-likelihood, which we minimize with gradient descent.

Stellar Applications

MDNs have many applications in astronomy. In stellar parameter inference, the same photometric observations can arise from different combinations of temperature, gravity and metallicity. Degeneracies and unmodeled effects such as extinction cause this. An MDN can provide posterior distributions over the stellar parameters instead of point estimates. These distributions show the uncertainty and a possible multimodality.

To train such an MDN we need pairs of stellar parameters and photometry. A stellar model can predict the photometry for given parameters, and this forward model generates the training pairs. The MDN then learns the inverse direction, from photometry to a distribution over the parameters. The posterior is only as good as the forward model, because the MDN learns it from the generated pairs.

Color-magnitude diagrams show complex multimodal distributions, because different stellar populations and evolutionary stages overlap. MDNs can model these structures, which allows more accurate stellar population analysis and distance determinations. In cosmological parameter estimation, MDNs can model the conditional distribution of the cosmological parameters given summary statistics of the observations. The conditional distribution represents degeneracies and constraints in parameter space, and it fits the Bayesian analysis that is widely used in modern cosmological inference.

These applications are early examples of simulation-based inference, which we meet in the last section of this chapter. There neural networks learn to approximate complex likelihoods or posteriors from simulated data.

15.13 Modern Neural Density Estimators

Mixture Density Networks are one of several neural density estimators. A neural density estimator uses a neural network to estimate a probability density function, either joint or conditional. The other estimators address limitations of MDNs and open new ways to model probabilistic relationships in scientific data. Many scientific applications need the full probabilistic relationship between variables, because it gives us the uncertainty.

MDNs rely on a specific parametric form, the Gaussian mixture model. This form is flexible, but it may need many components to approximate a complex distribution accurately. Each added component increases the number of parameters to estimate, which can lead to overfitting with limited data.

More fundamentally, the Gaussian assumption may not match the structure of scientific data. Cosmic ray hits can give measurement errors with heavy tails. Some physical processes generate distributions with sharp boundaries, which Gaussians represent poorly. Forcing a Gaussian mixture on such data may bias the results.

The limits of MDNs led to neural density estimators that represent complex distributions without a fixed parametric family. They rest on the same idea. Suppose we can transform a complex distribution into a simple one, such as a standard Gaussian. Then we can estimate densities by working in reverse, from the simple distribution back to the complex one. This idea connects to optimal transport theory, which studies efficient ways to transform one distribution into another.

Cosmology suggests an analogy. The universe began as a nearly Gaussian random field, similar to the Gaussian processes of Chapter 14. Gravitational evolution turned it into the complex, non-Gaussian structures we observe today. Neural density estimators attempt to reverse this process. They learn transformations that map complex distributions back to simple ones, or the other way round. Three approaches use this principle, normalizing flows, diffusion models and flow matching.

Normalizing Flows

A normalizing flow learns an invertible mapping between a simple base distribution, typically a standard Gaussian, and a complex target distribution. Invertibility is the main requirement, because we must be able to transform in both directions.

The flow rests on the transformation of random variables of Chapter 3. Let \(\mathbf{z}\) be a random variable with known density \(p_Z(\mathbf{z})\), and let \(f\) be an invertible function that gives \(\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{z})\). The density of \(\mathbf{y}\) is then \[ p_Y(\mathbf{y}) = p_Z(f^{-1}(\mathbf{y})) \left| \det\left( \frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \right) \right|. \] The Jacobian determinant term accounts for how the transformation stretches or compresses space, so that probability mass is conserved.

We parameterize \(f\) as a neural network that remains invertible, and so we can learn complex distributions directly from data. The base distribution is simple, so we easily evaluate probabilities and generate samples. The network maps it to the target distribution, where evaluation and sampling would otherwise be difficult. Figure 15.25 illustrates this mapping for a one-dimensional density.

In one dimension we know such a map already, the inverse CDF method of Chapter 12. For a target with CDF \(F_Y\) and a standard Gaussian with CDF \(\Phi\), the map \(f(z) = F_Y^{-1}(\Phi(z))\) is invertible and carries the Gaussian into the target. Figure 15.25 shows this map. In many dimensions the inverse CDF method has difficulties, and a flow learns such a map instead.

A flow gives both exact density evaluation and efficient sampling. To evaluate a density, we map an observed data point back to the base distribution and apply the formula above. To sample, we draw from the base distribution and map the samples to the target distribution.

However, the requirement of invertibility limits the neural networks we can use. Not all transformations are invertible. Among those that are, not all have a tractable inverse or a tractable Jacobian determinant. Flows therefore use specialized architectures that give up some expressivity to stay invertible.

In practice a flow is a stack of many simple invertible layers. Each layer makes a simple change to the density, and together the layers build the full transformation step by step. The intermediate stages of Figure 15.25 show such a gradual change.

Diffusion Models

The invertibility requirement leads to an alternative. Diffusion models transform between simple and complex distributions without a single invertible transformation.

A diffusion model gradually turns a complex distribution into a simple Gaussian. It does so in many small steps that each add noise. This forward process is a Markov chain (Chapter 13). A predefined schedule sets the amount of Gaussian noise that each step adds. One step reads \[ x_t = \sqrt{1-\beta_t}x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\varepsilon, \] where \(x_t\) is the data at time step \(t\) and \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathrm{Id})\) is random Gaussian noise. The noise schedule \(\beta_t\) is a small number that typically increases with \(t\).

As \(t\) approaches the final time step \(T\), the distribution of \(x_t\) approaches a standard Gaussian, whatever the initial data distribution is. The noise schedule is designed so that after enough steps the accumulated noise leaves almost no trace of the structure of the original data. Figure 15.26 shows how repeated noising turns a complex distribution into a Gaussian.

A neural network is trained to reverse this process. The noises of the steps combine into one Gaussian noise, so we compute \(x_t\) from \(x_0\) in one step with a single draw \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathrm{Id})\). The network learns to predict this \(\varepsilon\) from \(x_t\) and \(t\). The training goal is \[ \hat{\varepsilon}_{\mathbf{w}}(x_t, t) \approx \varepsilon, \] where \(\hat{\varepsilon}_{\mathbf{w}}\) is the neural network with parameters \(\mathbf{w}\).

This is the denoising task of Section 15.10, where an autoencoder learns to remove noise, here repeated at many noise levels. By predicting and removing this noise step by step, the model can turn a pure Gaussian sample back into a sample from the target distribution. Figure 15.26 shows this reverse chain for the bimodal density.

The main idea is to break the transformation into many small steps. This lets us turn a complex distribution into a Gaussian without requiring invertibility of the full transformation. Given the original data, the noised data follow a known Gaussian distribution, so each step only needs to model the noise component. Standard neural network architectures then work without invertibility constraints, and diffusion models allow a wider choice of architecture than normalizing flows.

The trade-off has two parts. Sampling from a diffusion model typically takes many steps, often hundreds or thousands of denoising iterations for one sample. This is expensive compared with the single pass of a normalizing flow. The random steps also give no direct reading of the density, which a normalizing flow provides exactly. However, the quality of the samples often justifies these costs for many applications.

A diffusion model can be trained on simulated pairs of parameters and observations and then generate parameter values for a given observation. Bayesian inference, however, often needs the density of the posterior or the likelihood, which a diffusion model does not give directly. The denoising network also estimates the score, the gradient of the log density. The score gives a route to the density, but only with extra computing and approximations. This limits the use of diffusion models in simulation-based inference (Section 15.14).

Flow Matching

Normalizing flows and diffusion models trade expressivity against a direct reading of the likelihood. A normalizing flow gives the exact density but restricts the network, and a diffusion model allows any network but gives no direct density. Flow matching takes an idea from each. It moves points deterministically from a Gaussian to the target distribution, as a normalizing flow does. It trains a free choice of network by a simple regression, as a diffusion model does. This has made flow matching a popular alternative to diffusion models.

Flow matching moves points along a velocity field \(v(x, t)\), which gives the velocity at position \(x\) and time \(t\). Moving points along this field solves an ordinary differential equation, and the resulting flow is invertible by construction. The network that models \(v\) therefore needs no invertibility constraint.

Training uses pairs of a data point \(x_0\) and a noise point \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathrm{Id})\). For a time \(t\) between 0 and 1, we join them by a straight line \[ x_t = (1 - t)\,x_0 + t\,\varepsilon. \] Along this line the point moves from the data point at \(t = 0\) to the noise point at \(t = 1\), with the constant velocity \(\varepsilon - x_0\). A network \(v_{\mathbf{w}}(x_t, t)\) learns to predict this velocity by minimizing the squared error \[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \left\| v_{\mathbf{w}}(x_t, t) - (\varepsilon - x_0) \right\|^2 \right], \] where the average runs over data points, noise points and times.

At a given position \(x\) and time \(t\), the straight lines of many different pairs cross, each with its own velocity. The network sees only \(x\) and \(t\), not which line the point is on. Its best prediction is therefore the average velocity of all lines through that point. This average is the field the network learns, and following it carries the Gaussian into the data distribution. The paths that follow this field are the flow lines, and unlike the straight lines they cannot cross. Figure 15.27 shows this field and its flow lines for a bimodal density.

To sample, we draw a point from the Gaussian at \(t = 1\) and follow the differential equation \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t = v_{\mathbf{w}}(x, t)\) back to \(t = 0\) with a numerical solver. Only sampling needs this solver. Training is the regression above. The flow lines are gentle curves, so sampling often needs fewer steps than a diffusion model. Because the flow is invertible, we can also compute the density of a sample, as a normalizing flow does.

Flow matching and diffusion models are closely related. A diffusion model follows a stochastic process, in which each step adds random noise. Flow matching follows an ordinary differential equation with a velocity field, so its paths are deterministic. Both connect data to noise, but flow matching also allows other choices of path, such as straight lines. Flow matching is still little explored in astronomy.

MDNs, normalizing flows, diffusion models and flow matching all use neural networks to model probability distributions. Their implementations differ, but they have the same goal, which is density estimation and sampling for complex distributions.

In astronomy, these methods can model complex observational processes, account for selection effects, and generate synthetic data sets with the statistical properties of real observations.

Normalizing flows have been used to model the distribution of galaxy properties in large surveys. They describe complex correlations between mass, color and morphology that simple parametric models miss. Diffusion models have given encouraging results for generating synthetic astronomical images. These images can keep realistic noise properties and subtle correlations across wavelengths.

Neural density estimators are becoming standard in modern astrostatistics. This holds especially for simulation-based inference, where complex physical models must be connected with observational data. These methods can work with high-dimensional data directly or with summary statistics. With the full data they can extract more information and still keep a sound statistical basis.

The field evolves rapidly, and new architectures and training methods appear regularly. Neural networks that learn complex probability distributions give scientific inference more flexibility than parametric methods do. They keep the probabilistic treatment of uncertainty.

15.14 Simulation-Based Inference

Simulation-based inference (SBI) is an application of neural density estimators. It connects complex scientific theories with observations. SBI addresses a challenge of modern astronomy, which is Bayesian inference when the theoretical models are so complex that analytical likelihood functions become intractable.

The Likelihood Problem

Bayesian inference (Chapter 2) needs a likelihood function \(p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\), which gives the probability of the data \(\mathbf{x}\) given the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). We combine it with a prior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) to compute the posterior distribution \[ p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}). \]

This works well when we can write down the likelihood function explicitly. As scientific models become more sophisticated, an analytical likelihood becomes hard or impossible to specify. Modern cosmological simulations are an example. Given cosmological parameters, we can run numerical simulations that generate synthetic observations such as galaxy distributions or weak lensing maps. Typically, however, we cannot write a closed-form expression for the probability of a specific observed outcome.

The core issue is dimensionality and distributional complexity. A galaxy density field represented as an image is high dimensional. A modest \(512 \times 512\) pixel image lives in a space with 262,144 dimensions. In such a space, characterizing the distribution \(p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\) explicitly becomes intractable. The distribution typically has complex multimodality, strong correlations and heavy tails, which resist a simple parametric representation.

Over the past decades, astronomy has made much progress in simulating complex physical systems, from cosmological structure formation to stellar evolution. Advances in high-performance computing and numerical methods made this possible. The simulations include more detailed physics and reach higher resolution. A gap has remained in how to connect the simulations to observational data in a statistically sound way.

Traditionally, astronomers reduce the dimensionality with summary statistics. Low-dimensional summaries such as power spectra or correlation functions condense the high-dimensional observations into a more manageable statistical problem. By the central limit theorem, these summary statistics often have distributions closer to Gaussian. Techniques such as the Laplace approximation (Chapter 9) then apply more readily.

This convenience has a cost, which is information loss. The power spectrum describes only certain aspects of the data, namely the second moments of the distribution. For a Gaussian random field, the power spectrum is a complete statistical description. Cosmic structures and other astronomical phenomena, however, are non-Gaussian. Their higher-order moments and phase correlations carry information that the power spectrum discards.

This is a dilemma between tractability and completeness. Full high-dimensional observations preserve all available information, but the likelihood becomes practically incalculable. Summary statistics give tractable inference problems, but they may sacrifice information. For cosmic structure no single summary statistic keeps all the information, but whether a few together keep nearly all of it is less clear. Astronomers have therefore made pragmatic compromises, typically favoring tractability over statistical power.

SBI resolves this dilemma by using an asymmetry common to many scientific domains. The forward problem, which generates observations from parameters by simulation, is tractable. The inverse problem, which infers parameters from observations, is hard. SBI uses neural networks to learn surrogates, which are fast approximations, of the main components of the Bayesian inference pipeline directly from simulated data.

SBI does not force a choice between the two sides of this dilemma. We can apply it to the full observations, and cosmologists call such an analysis field-level inference. We can also apply it to summary statistics whose likelihood we cannot write down. SBI also differs from emulation, which is common in cosmology. An emulator typically predicts the mean observable for given parameters, for example a power spectrum, and replaces a slow simulation. SBI instead learns the distribution of the observable or of the parameters.

The SBI workflow begins with simulation. Consider a cosmological example. We want to infer parameters from observations of the cosmic web. The parameters include the matter density \(\Omega_m\), the dark energy equation of state \(w\) and the amplitude of fluctuations \(\sigma_8\). We generate parameter-observation pairs \(\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}_i, \mathbf{x}_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) in two steps.

  1. Sample cosmological parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = (\Omega_m, w, \sigma_8, ...)_i\) from a prior distribution \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\).

  2. Run cosmological simulations with these parameters to generate synthetic galaxy density fields \(\mathbf{x}_i\).

With simulations first, we need no analytical likelihood function. We use the simulated data to train neural networks that approximate either the likelihood \(p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\) or the posterior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x})\) directly. Figure 15.28 shows the simulated pairs and the two distributions that we can learn from them.

Neural Likelihood Estimation

Neural likelihood estimation (NLE) is the most straightforward approach to SBI in principle. It learns the likelihood function \(p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\) directly. This keeps the structure of standard Bayesian inference and extends it to problems that were intractable. The learned likelihood replaces the analytical one and fits into the rest of the Bayesian analysis.

We can implement NLE with the neural density estimators of the previous section. With an MDN, for example, we model the likelihood as \[ p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\boldsymbol{\theta}), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k(\boldsymbol{\theta})). \]

Training follows maximum likelihood. Given the simulated parameter-observation pairs, we maximize \[ \ell(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln p(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\theta}_i, \mathbf{w}), \] where \(\mathbf{w}\) denotes the neural network parameters.

For high-dimensional observations such as galaxy density fields, we might use normalizing flows, diffusion models or flow matching instead of MDNs. The principle stays the same. We learn a mapping from the parameters to a distribution of observations, which encodes complex physics in a differentiable probabilistic model.

NLE preserves the modular nature of Bayesian inference. We can change the prior, combine the likelihood with other likelihood terms, or use a different sampling method without retraining the neural likelihood. We still run MCMC for each new observation, but each likelihood evaluation is now a fast forward pass through the network. However, high-dimensional observations are costly to model. Predicting distributions in such a high-dimensional observation space needs enormous neural networks.

Neural Posterior Estimation

This dimensionality challenge leads to neural posterior estimation (NPE). NPE takes a more direct route and approximates the posterior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x})\) with a conditional density estimator. By modeling the posterior instead of the likelihood, we only predict distributions in the much lower-dimensional parameter space.

The observation \(\mathbf{x}\) might be a \(512 \times 512\) pixel density field, while \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) might hold just 5 to 10 cosmological parameters. The network takes the observations \(\mathbf{x}\) as input and outputs a distribution over the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). This makes NPE computationally more efficient and statistically more feasible.

The two methods differ in what they model. NLE asks, “Given parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), what observations \(\mathbf{x}\) might we see?” NPE asks, “Given observations \(\mathbf{x}\), what parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) might have generated them?”

NPE gives posteriors directly, without evaluating a likelihood or running MCMC. Inference is therefore very fast once the network is trained. However, the network implicitly contains the prior used in training. To explore other priors later, we must retrain the network or correct the result with importance sampling (Chapter 12). This trade-off suits applications with well-established priors that are unlikely to change. It also suits applications where inference speed matters most, such as analyzing millions of galaxy spectra from large surveys.

Amortized Inference

Both NLE and NPE enable amortized inference. Traditionally we run MCMC again for each new observation, which is expensive when each likelihood evaluation needs extensive calculation. In amortized inference, we train a neural network once to approximate either the likelihood or the posterior. We then reuse the approximation for many observations without retraining. The word amortized means that we pay the training cost once and spread it over later observations, so the advantage grows with their number.

Inference without explicit likelihood functions is an old idea. Approximate Bayesian computation had similar goals. It compares summary statistics of simulated and observed data and accepts the parameter values whose simulations are “close enough” to the observations. However, these methods scaled poorly and often needed careful manual design of the summary statistics and distance metrics. Modern SBI methods differ because neural density estimation has advanced. The deep learning innovations behind generative AI make it possible to approximate high-dimensional, multimodal distributions reliably and at scale.

Early neural approaches often suffered from mode collapse. In mode collapse, the network generates samples from only one or a few modes of a multimodal distribution. It misses other equally valid regions of high probability. For a distribution with three distinct peaks, for example, a neural network with mode collapse might represent one peak and ignore the others. Normalizing flows, diffusion models and flow matching reduce this problem. Their architectures and training procedures better preserve the multimodal structure.

SBI applies well beyond cosmology, to other areas with complex forward models but intractable likelihoods. In stellar population synthesis, we can infer stellar population properties from integrated galaxy spectra. In exoplanet characterization, we can determine atmospheric compositions from transmission spectra. In gravitational wave analysis, we can infer properties of merging compact objects from the signals.

Caveats

SBI has caveats. The neural surrogate is valid only within the parameter space used for training. Its accuracy depends on how well the training simulations represent reality. When we apply SBI to the full observations, we use information at all scales and also include more systematic effects. For example, cosmological simulations may not model baryon physics accurately at all scales. Applying SBI blindly, especially in field-level inference, might then give overconfident inferences that depend on these systematic effects.

All simulation-based methods face the same problem. We address it with testing and validation, namely benchmarking, blind tests and systematic error analysis. We generate additional simulations with varied physical assumptions to assess the sensitivity to modeling choices. We can also train on one set of simulations and test on others, which measures the impact of systematic effects.

Using the full observations does not always increase the systematic errors compared with summary statistics. In some cases, biases might average out. This remains an active research area. These problems call for careful scientific methodology, and we can still use SBI.

A last caveat concerns the network itself. Cross-validation estimates the prediction error of a neural network, but it does not fully account for the uncertainty of the network parameters themselves. Even so, the approximation errors of modern neural density estimators are often smaller than the observational noise and the systematic effects of the simulations. We can then focus on the physical questions and on the familiar tests above, now with more information from the observations.

15.15 Tutorials: Backpropagation, Autoencoders and Neural Density Estimators

The four tutorials build up from the mechanics of training to networks that predict and model whole densities. The first writes backpropagation by hand and then uses PyTorch, a Python library that computes gradients automatically. The second compresses galaxy images with an autoencoder. The third predicts the lithium abundance of stars with a mixture density network. The fourth models the elemental abundances of stars with a normalizing flow. The full tutorials can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as 15a to 15d.

Backpropagation and PyTorch

Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, and a network can have millions of weights. Backpropagation instead computes all the gradients in one backward pass (Section 15.4). The pass applies the chain rule from the loss back to each weight and reuses the numbers that the forward pass stored. The first tutorial writes this backward pass by hand for a small network that fits a noisy cubic.

PyTorch then computes the same gradients by automatic differentiation, from the forward pass alone. The hand-written gradients agree with those of PyTorch for the same weights (Figure 15.29b), and both networks follow the cubic (Figure 15.29a). PyTorch also provides common optimizers, so we can compare them on the same network. With the same mini-batches and number of epochs, Adam (Section 15.3) reaches a much lower loss than stochastic gradient descent (Figure 15.29c). Adam rescales the step of each parameter by the size of its recent gradients, so parameters with small gradients still move.

The chain rule, the two passes and a gradient-based optimizer are most of what even very large networks need. A library supplies the backward pass for any model we write, so the other three tutorials can focus on the models.

Autoencoders for Galaxy Images

Principal component analysis (PCA) of Chapter 10 compresses an image with a linear map. An elongated or tilted galaxy, however, spreads over several components (Section 10.10). An autoencoder (Section 15.10) replaces the linear map with neural networks. An encoder compresses each image into a few numbers, and a decoder rebuilds the image from them. Because the networks are nonlinear, these numbers can follow curved structure that a linear map misses.

A network this flexible can also memorize its training images. We therefore stop the training where the error on separate validation images is lowest (Section 15.3). On test images the reconstructions keep the size, shape and orientation of each galaxy, as with PCA, and are slightly sharper (Figure 15.30a). The training error ends below that of any linear map of the same size, so the network represents structure that PCA misses (Figure 15.30b).

An autoencoder thus learns a compact, nonlinear description of large images from the images alone, without labels. Galaxies that it rebuilds poorly differ from its training sample, so the reconstruction error can also flag unusual objects.

Lithium Abundance in Open Clusters

Lithium burns in the hot layers below the surface, so a star destroys the lithium that convection carries there. The lithium abundance A(Li) of a star therefore depends on its temperature, which sets the depth of convection, and on its age. It also depends on unmeasured properties such as rotation, so stars of the same temperature and age differ in A(Li). The third tutorial uses stars of open clusters, whose ages are known.

A standard network predicts one value of A(Li) for each temperature and age. With the squared error as its loss, that value is the mean of the stars with these inputs. The mean loses the scatter and any second branch of the data (Section 15.12). A mixture density network (MDN) instead predicts the mixture weights, means and widths of a Gaussian mixture as functions of the inputs. We train it by maximizing the likelihood of the observed abundances.

The tutorial first tests the network on the two moons, two interleaved half circles. Some values of \(x\) have two values of \(y\), one on each moon. A standard network would predict their average, on neither moon, while the MDN gives each moon its own component (Figure 15.31a).

For the stars, the network predicts a density of A(Li) at each temperature and age. Its mean falls toward cooler stars, whose convection reaches deeper, and with age, because the burning continues (Figure 15.31b). Its width, which holds what temperature and age leave unexplained, grows with age, most for the cool stars (Figure 15.31c).

A network can therefore predict a whole probability density rather than one value. Many quantities in astronomy have a scatter that changes with the inputs, or more than one possible value. For them the predicted width is itself a result.

Chemical Abundances with a Normalizing Flow

The elemental abundances of stars in the Milky Way form sequences, such as the two sequences of [Mg/Fe] against [Fe/H] (Figure 15.32a). Massive-star supernovae make magnesium and mainly enrich the upper sequence, while Type Ia supernovae also add iron to the gas of the lower one. The fourth tutorial models 13 abundances of APOGEE stars together, as a density in 13 dimensions. A Gaussian has one peak, however, and a mixture needs many components for curved sequences in many dimensions.

A normalizing flow instead transforms a standard Gaussian into the density of the stars with an invertible network (Section 15.13). The change of variables gives its exact likelihood, which we maximize on the stars. We build its most basic form, RealNVP, whose layers freeze some abundances and scale and shift the others with networks of the frozen ones. The inverse needs no inverted network, and the Jacobian is triangular and cheap.

Samples of the flow follow both sequences and keep a lower density between them (Figure 15.32b). This plane is one view of the 13 dimensions, and the samples follow the stars in the other views too.

A normalizing flow represents a density without a fixed parametric family, unlike the Gaussian mixture of an MDN. It gives both the likelihood of a star and mock stars, and it scales to many dimensions. This makes it a basis for density estimation in astronomy and for simulation-based inference (Section 15.14).

McCulloch and Pitts (1943) described neural computation with a mathematical model. Rosenblatt (1958) introduced the perceptron, and Minsky and Papert (1969) analyzed the limits of single-layer networks. Rumelhart et al. (1986) presented backpropagation. Kingma and Ba (2015) introduced the Adam optimizer, which uses moving averages of the gradient and its square. Cybenko (1989) and Hornik et al. (1989) studied universal approximation, and Vapnik (1995) placed neural networks in statistical learning theory. MacKay (1992) applied the Bayesian evidence to regularization and model comparison. Neal (1996) gave a full Bayesian treatment of networks, and Williams (1996) related them to Gaussian processes. LeCun et al. (1998) described convolutional networks, Elman (1990) recurrent networks and Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) long short-term memory. He et al. (2016) introduced residual networks, whose shortcut connections make very deep networks easier to train. Vaswani et al. (2017) introduced the Transformer, a network built on attention without recurrence or convolution. Bishop (1994) introduced mixture density networks, and Hinton et al. (2012) and Srivastava et al. (2014) developed dropout. Astronomers applied neural networks early. Storrie-Lombardi et al. (1992) classified galaxy morphology, and von Hippel et al. (1994) classified stellar spectra. Lahav et al. (1995) compared networks with human classifiers, and Bailer-Jones et al. (1998) classified spectral type and luminosity class. Belkin et al. (2019) described double descent, Nakkiran et al. (2019) showed it in deep learning, and Adlam and Pennington (2020) analyzed it. Jacot et al. (2018) introduced the neural tangent kernel, and Lee et al. (2017) and Matthews et al. (2018) related wide networks to Gaussian processes. Cranmer et al. (2020) review simulation-based inference, and Papamakarios et al. (2018) examined neural likelihood estimation. Greenberg et al. (2019) and Gonçalves et al. (2020) developed neural posterior estimation. Bommasani et al. (2021) review large pre-trained models. Brown et al. (2020) showed that large language models learn from few examples. Wei et al. (2022) analyzed abilities that appear only in large models. Devlin et al. (2018) and Raffel et al. (2020) examined pre-training and transfer learning. Kingma and Welling (2013) introduced variational autoencoders. Goodfellow et al. (2014) introduced generative adversarial networks, in which two networks compete, and Rezende and Mohamed (2015) normalizing flows. Dinh et al. (2016) and Durkan et al. (2019) developed them further. Ho et al. (2020) introduced denoising diffusion models, and Song et al. (2020) unified them with score-based generative models. Ting and Weinberg (2022) used a normalizing flow on the APOGEE stars of the fourth tutorial to study the intrinsic dimensionality of the abundances. Sun et al. (2025) trained a mixture density network on the open clusters of the third tutorial and studied lithium in comoving pairs of stars.
